review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Prebiotics are specific types of dietary fibers or fermentable substrates that beneficial gut microbes use as fuel. Unlike probiotics, which are live microorganisms ingested to confer health benefits, prebiotics nourish and selectively stimulate the growth and activity of advantageous microbes already present in the gastrointestinal tract. Major mechanisms include fermentation of prebiotic fibers by gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate, acetate, and propionate. These metabolites help maintain gut barrier function, modulate inflammation, and provide energy to colon cells. Common natural food sources of prebiotics include garlic, onions, leeks, asparagus, bananas, and whole grains containing inulin, fructooligosaccharides, and galactooligosaccharides. Prebiotics have practical relevance in promoting digestive health, supporting immune function, and potentially reducing risk factors for metabolic and inflammatory diseases. However, individual responses vary, and consuming excessive amounts may cause digestive discomfort like gas and bloating. Emerging evidence continues to explore the role of prebiotics in systemic health beyond the gut. Understanding the distinction between prebiotics and probiotics, selecting appropriate food sources, and considering balanced intake are important considerations for consumers and healthcare providers.
